summary: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage by scavenging free radicals. It is used to prevent and treat vitamin E deficiency, which occurs mainly in fat-malabsorption states (cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, abetalipoproteinemia) and in premature infants. Deficiency causes neuromuscular and haemolytic problems. It is generally very safe at recommended intakes, but high-dose supplementation can increase bleeding risk (especially with anticoagulants) and has been associated with adverse outcomes.
indications: Prevention and treatment of vitamin E deficiency
Vitamin E deficiency due to fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, chronic cholestasis, abetalipoproteinemia)
Nutritional supplementation, including in premature/low-birth-weight infants
Dietary supplement to meet recommended intake

dosage.d: 15 mg (approximately 22.4 IU natural / 33 IU synthetic) daily
Higher oral doses individualized (e.g., up to 100-200 IU/kg/day in severe malabsorption)
dosage.n: Water-miscible forms preferred in cholestasis; titrate to serum levels
Do not exceed long-term without supervision
Used to prevent deficiency-related haemolytic anemia

admin: Take with food, ideally containing some fat, to maximize absorption
Use water-miscible (TPGS) formulations in patients with severe fat malabsorption or cholestasis
Separate from agents that may reduce absorption (e.g., bile-acid sequestrants, orlistat)
Do not exceed the tolerable upper intake without medical advice
moa: Alpha-tocopherol is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that incorporates into cell membranes and lipoproteins, where it donates a hydrogen atom to neutralize peroxyl free radicals and terminate lipid peroxidation chain reactions. This protects polyunsaturated membrane fatty acids, red cell membranes and neural tissue from oxidative damage. It is regenerated by vitamin C and other antioxidants.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to vitamin E or product excipients
relative: Bleeding disorders or vitamin K deficiency
monitor: Signs of bleeding with high-dose use

preg: At recommended dietary intakes vitamin E is safe and necessary in pregnancy. Routine high-dose supplementation is not recommended and has not shown benefit; avoid megadoses.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding at recommended intakes; vitamin E is a normal component of breast milk.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual intakes.
hepatic: Adequate bile and normal hepatic/biliary function are needed for absorption; chronic cholestatic liver disease causes malabsorption and may require water-soluble formulations and higher doses.

major: Oral anticoagulants/warfarin (high-dose vitamin E increases bleeding risk - monitor INR)
moderate: Antiplatelet agents (additive bleeding risk at high doses)
Orlistat, cholestyramine, colestipol (reduce vitamin E absorption)
Vitamin K (high vitamin E doses may antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting)
interactions.food: Dietary fat enhances absorption; high-fat meal recommended
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use can worsen fat-soluble vitamin status
interactions.diagnostics: High doses may affect coagulation tests (INR)

common: Generally well tolerated at recommended doses
serious: Increased bleeding tendency (high doses, especially with anticoagulants)
Possible increased risk of haemorrhagic stroke with very high long-term doses
rare: Necrotizing enterocolitis association in preterm infants (historically with certain IV preparations)
emergency: Severe bleeding/haemorrhage with megadoses plus anticoagulation

monitoring: Serum alpha-tocopherol levels in malabsorption or supplementation for deficiency
Signs of bleeding and coagulation parameters when high doses combine with anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Growth and neurologic status in children treated for deficiency
counsel: Take with food for best absorption
More is not better - avoid very high doses unless advised, as they can increase bleeding risk
Tell your doctor if you take blood thinners or are scheduled for surgery
Stop high-dose supplements before planned surgery as advised
A balanced diet (vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, green vegetables) usually meets requirements
pk: Antioxidant activity once absorbed and distributed into membranes
Plasma concentrations peak several hours after an oral dose
Long body retention; plasma half-life of alpha-tocopherol roughly 2 days, with large adipose stores
Stored in adipose tissue and liver, providing prolonged reserves
Store at room temperature, protected from light and air (oxidation)
pearls: Alpha-tocopherol is the only form maintained in human plasma by the hepatic alpha-tocopherol transfer protein
Deficiency is rare and almost always due to fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, abetalipoproteinemia) rather than poor diet
1 mg RRR-alpha-tocopherol = 1.49 IU natural source; synthetic dl-alpha-tocopherol is less potent
High-dose supplementation can potentiate warfarin and may increase haemorrhagic stroke risk - it is not a benign 'more is better' vitamin
Use water-miscible forms in cholestatic patients who cannot absorb the fat-soluble form
missed: For routine supplementation, take the missed dose when remembered, or skip it if it is almost time for the next dose. Do not double up. Occasional missed doses are not harmful because vitamin E is stored in the body.
overdose: Acute toxicity is low. Chronic excessive intake (well above the upper limit) may cause nausea, diarrhea, fatigue and, importantly, an increased bleeding tendency that may be marked in those on anticoagulants or with vitamin K deficiency. Management is to stop supplementation and provide supportive care; vitamin K may be given for significant bleeding.
